findings.reason: Correct. Merged with ADV-15. Roth IRA: the applicable dollar amount for a married person filing separately is zero (26 U.S.C. 408A(c)(3)(B)(ii)(III)), so 'Roth IRA eligibility' is in the list. Income-driven loans: under 34 CFR 685.209(e)(1) as in force 2026-11-01 (which covers the new Repayment Assistance Plan as well as IBR/PAYE/REPAYE/ICR), a married borrower filing separately is assessed on own income only, so filing separately can lower the payment; that is stated. The trade-off (separate returns generally lose the EITC and the premium tax credit, 26 U.S.C. 32(d)(1) and 36B(c)(1)(C), with narrow separated-spouse and domestic-abuse exceptions) is stated with 'generally'. P.L. 119-21 was grepped for amendments to 32(d), 36B(c)(1)(C) and 408A(c)(3); none found.

blocks.body: Marriage opens a special enrollment period (at least 30 days for employer plans, 60 days on the Marketplace). Compare both employers' plans on premium plus expected out-of-pocket cost, including any spousal surcharge. If one of you contributes to an HSA, a general-purpose health FSA at the other's job that can pay your expenses makes you ineligible to contribute; a limited-purpose FSA does not, so check before electing.
blocks.plain: Getting married opens a special window to change health plans: at least 30 days for job-based plans and 60 days on the Marketplace. Compare both employers' plans by premium plus the costs you expect to pay yourself, including any extra charge for covering a spouse. If one of you puts money in an HSA (health savings account), a regular health FSA (flexible spending account) at the other spouse's job that can pay your bills means you can't add to the HSA. A limited-purpose FSA does not cause this problem, so check before you sign up.

blocks.body: Your filing status is set by whether you are married on December 31, so a December wedding counts for the whole year. Two incomes withheld as if each were single often under-withhold once combined; run the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator together and file new W-4s. Marriage can also change the EITC, Marketplace premium credits, Medicaid, SSI, income-driven student-loan payments and Roth IRA eligibility. Filing separately keeps a spouse's income out of an income-driven loan payment but generally rules out the EITC and premium credits, so compare both returns before choosing.
blocks.plain: Whether you count as married for taxes depends on December 31. So a December wedding counts for the whole year. Two paychecks each taxed as if single often don't have enough tax taken out once you're combined. Use the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator together and file new W-4s. Getting married can also change the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), help paying for Marketplace health insurance, Medicaid, SSI, income-driven student loan payments, and whether you can put money in a Roth IRA. Filing separate tax returns keeps your spouse's income out of an income-driven loan payment. But it usually means no EITC and no help with Marketplace premiums, so compare both ways before you choose.

blocks.body: Retirement accounts and life insurance pass by beneficiary form, not by will. In a 401(k), federal law generally makes a spouse the default beneficiary unless they waive in writing; a waiver in a prenuptial agreement does not count, so the spouse has to consent after the wedding. IRAs follow whatever the form says. Read each form rather than assuming, and review your will, power of attorney and healthcare directive at the same time.
blocks.plain: Retirement accounts and life insurance go to whoever is named on the beneficiary form, not to whoever is named in a will. In a 401(k), federal law generally makes your spouse the default beneficiary unless they give that up in writing. Giving it up in a prenup does not count, so your spouse has to sign after the wedding. IRAs go to whoever the form names. Read every form instead of assuming, and look over your will, power of attorney and healthcare directive at the same time.

new_claims.claim: An individual covered by a general-purpose health FSA (including one sponsored by a spouse's employer) that pays or reimburses medical expenses is not an HSA-eligible individual; a limited-purpose health FSA does not disqualify
new_claims.source: 26 U.S.C. §223(c)(1)(A)(ii); Rev. Rul. 2004-45 (I.R.B. 2004-22); IRS Publication 969 (2025), 'Other employee health plans'
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: 26 U.S.C. §223(c)(1)(A)(ii) (not eligible while covered by any other health plan that is not an HDHP); Rev. Rul. 2004-45: 'This result is the same if the individual is covered by a health FSA or HRA sponsored by the employer of the individual's spouse'; Pub. 969 lists the limited-purpose health FSA as permitted. P.L. 119-21 §§71306, 71308 amended §223(c)(1) only for telehealth and direct primary care. Added from the §4.4 persona pass (CFP-16).

new_claims.claim: A married taxpayer can claim the EITC or the premium tax credit generally only on a joint return; a married individual filing separately has a Roth IRA applicable dollar amount of zero
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: §32(d)(1) ('In the case of an individual who is married, this section shall apply only if a joint return is filed'), with the §32(d)(2)(B) separated-spouse exception; §36B(c)(1)(C) (applicable taxpayer only if the spouses file a joint return) and 26 CFR §1.36B-2(b)(2)(ii) (domestic abuse and abandonment exception); §408A(c)(3)(B)(ii)(III) (applicable dollar amount zero for a married individual filing a separate return). Exceptions are why the content says 'generally'. govinfo text is the 2024 edition; P.L. 119-21 was searched and does not amend these provisions. Added from the §4.4 persona pass (ADV-15, CFP-17). Checker 2026-11-16: §408A(c)(3)(C) applies §219(g)(4), so a married individual who files separately and lives apart from the spouse all year is not treated as married for the Roth limit; another reason the content says 'can change' rather than stating a bar.

new_claims.claim: Medicaid MAGI rules place a spouse living with the applicant in the same household regardless of tax filing; SSI deems the income and resources of an ineligible spouse living in the same household to the applicant
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: 42 CFR §435.603(f)(4) ('In the case of a married couple living together, each spouse will be included in the household of the other spouse, regardless of whether they expect to file a joint tax return'); 42 U.S.C. §1382c(f)(1) (income and resources 'shall be deemed to include any income and resources of such spouse'). The content says only that marriage 'can change' these; state Medicaid thresholds were not read. Added from the §4.4 persona pass (ADV-15).

new_claims.claim: For income-driven Direct Loan repayment (RAP, REPAYE, IBR, PAYE and ICR), a married borrower filing a separate federal return is assessed on the borrower's income only; on a joint return the combined income of borrower and spouse is used
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: 34 CFR §685.209(e)(1)(i)(A) ('a married borrower filing a separate Federal income tax return ... only the borrower's income is used in the calculation') and (e)(1)(i)(B) ('the combined income of the borrower and spouse is used'); (e)(1)(ii) applies the same rule to ICR except joint ICR repayment. FFEL-only IBR borrowers were not separately checked. Added from the §4.4 persona pass (CFP-17).

new_claims.claim: Spousal consent contained in a prenuptial (antenuptial) agreement does not satisfy the spousal consent requirements of IRC §401(a)(11) and §417
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: 26 CFR §1.401(a)-20 A-28: 'An agreement entered into prior to marriage does not satisfy the applicable consent requirements, even if the agreement is executed within the applicable election period.' Added from the §4.4 persona pass (CFP-18).

new_claims.claim: A creditor may not refuse to grant an individual account to a creditworthy applicant on the basis of marital status
new_claims.note: Verified 2026-11-16 at the primary source: 12 CFR §1002.7(a): 'A creditor shall not refuse to grant an individual account to a creditworthy applicant on the basis of sex, marital status, or any other prohibited basis.' The accompanying advice (keep an account and some credit in your own name) is a convention, not a legal requirement. Added from the §4.4 persona pass (ADV-16).
